items.answer:  (D) Both A and R are false Both statements are incorrect. The Mathura school used red sandstone and had a distinct Indian style. The Gandhara school used grey- black schist and showed Greco-Roman influence. The descriptions are swapped here.

items.stem: The Cheras exclusively traded with Central Asian empires over land. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.answer:  (A) 1 and 2 only The Cholas, Cheras, and Pandyas are indeed referred to as the “Muvendar” (Three Crowned Kings). Sangam literature is the earliest extant Tamil literature. The Cheras were known for maritime trade, especially with Rome.

items.stem: The Indo-Greek ambassador Heliodorus erected a famous pillar near Vidisha, dedicating it to the deity _____, whom he praised as ‘god of gods’.
items.answer:  (C) Vasudeva The Heliodorus pillar inscription explicitly states that it was erected by Heliodorus, an ambassador of an Indo-Greek king, in honor of Vasudeva (a form of Vishnu/Krishna), whom he revered as the “god of gods” (devadeva).

items.stem: What does “Shaka Samvat” refer to?

options.label: A
options.text: A style of Shaka period temple architecture

options.label: B
options.text: A calendar era initiated during Shaka rule

options.label: C
options.text: A specific type of coin issued by Shakas

options.label: D
options.text: A philosophical text written by Shaka one

items.answer:  (B) A calendar era initiated during Shaka rule The Shaka Samvat (Shaka Era) is a historical calendar era that is believed to have been initiated during the rule of the Shakas (Indo-Scythians) in India. It is still used as the Indian National Calendar.

items.stem: The flourishing of Sanskrit literature, including the final compilation of epics like the Mahabharata and Ramayana, during this “Age of Reorganisation” suggests what about the cultural environment? activity

options.label: A
options.text: A complete decline in all forms of learning

options.label: B
options.text: A period of significant literary and cultural

options.label: C
options.text: The exclusive use of Prakrit languages

options.label: D
options.text: A suppression of all epic storytelling forms

items.answer:  (B) A period of significant literary and cultural activity The compilation and flourishing of major Sanskrit literary works, including the great epics, indicates a vibrant cultural and intellectual environment during this period, with continued development and refinement of classical Indian traditions for all. MAT CHING TYPE QUESTION 

items.stem: Who is generally accepted as the last Maurya emperor’s assassin and founder of the Shunga dynasty?
items.answer:  Pushyamitra Shunga.

items.stem: Around what year BCE did the Maurya empire break up?
items.answer:  Around 185 BCE.

items.stem: What term do some scholars use for the post- Maurya period characterized by new competing kingdoms?
items.answer:  Age of reorganisation.

items.stem: What is an alliance arranged through marriage between royal families called?
items.answer:  Matrimonial alliance.

items.stem: Which Vedic ritual, involving a horse, did Pushyamitra Shunga perform to assert power?
items.answer:  Ashvamedha yajna.

items.stem: Which ancient text on Yoga was compiled by Patanjali during the Shunga period?
items.answer:  Yoga Sutras.

items.stem: Name the stupa in Madhya Pradesh known for its railings and reliefs added by the Shungas.
items.answer:  Bharhut Stupa.

items.stem: Which powerful dynasty, sometimes called ‘Andhras’, ruled large parts of the Deccan after the Mauryas?
items.answer:  Satavahanas.

items.stem: Name one famous capital city of the Satavahanas.
items.answer:  Amravati/Pratishthana (Paithan) (any one).

items.stem: What objects often depicted ships, suggesting significant Satavahana maritime trade?
items.answer:  Coins.

items.stem: Name the Satavahana king mentioned who was named after his mother, Gautami Balashri.
items.answer:  Gautamiputra Satakarni.

items.stem: In which caves near Pune were inscriptions found detailing a Satavahana queen’s rituals and donations?
items.answer:  Naneghat Caves. Click Here to Buy book on Amazon CH 06: The Age of Reorganisation

items.stem: Which dynasty rose to prominence in Kalinga after the Mauryas?
items.answer:  Chedi dynasty.

items.stem: Name the main Chedi ruler known from the Hathigumpha inscription.
items.answer:  Kharavela.

items.stem: Near which modern city are the Udayagiri- Khandagiri caves located?
items.answer:  Bhubaneswar.

items.stem: What collective name is given to the oldest Tamil literature from this era?
items.answer:  Sangam literature.

items.stem: What does the word ‘sangam’ (derived from sangha) mean in this context?
items.answer:  Association or assembly (of poets).

items.stem: Name the three ‘crowned kings’ or major kingdoms of the Sangam Age in the South.
items.answer:  Cholas, Cheras, and Pandyas.

items.stem: Which Chola king is credited with building the Kallanai (Grand Anicut)?
items.answer:  Karikala.

items.stem: What other name were the Cheras known by?
items.answer:  Keralaputra (‘sons of Kerala’).

items.stem: What group established kingdoms in Northwest India after Alexander’s satraps?
items.answer:  Indo-Greeks.

items.stem: Which group, also called Indo-Scythians, invaded after the Indo-Greeks?
items.answer:  Shakas.

items.stem: Which calendar system, adopted as India’s National Calendar, originated during the Shaka period?
items.answer:  Shaka Samvat.

items.stem: Which dynasty, originally from Central Asia, established a large empire including North India around the 2nd century CE?
items.answer:  Kushanas.

items.stem: Name the most powerful Kushana ruler, known from a famous headless statue.
items.answer:  Kanishka. SSHORT Answer QUESTIO 

items.stem: Why is the period following the Maurya empire sometimes called the ‘Age of Reorganisation’?
items.answer:  After the large, centralized Maurya empire collapsed, the subcontinent saw existing regions reorganised into numerous smaller, competing kingdoms, alongside invasions, leading to a new political map.

items.stem: Describe the purpose and process of the ashvamedha yajna ritual.
items.answer:  It was a Vedic ritual for rulers to declare supremacy. A special horse wandered freely; territories it crossed unchallenged became part of the king’s empire, while challenging it led to battle.

items.stem: What evidence shows Shunga patronage of art, despite the revival of Vedic practices?
items.answer:  The Shungas added beautifully carved railings and reliefs depicting Buddhist themes (like Jataka tales) to the existing Bharhut Stupa, showcasing their contribution to Buddhist art. NODIA

items.stem: How do Satavahana coins indicate the importance of trade, particularly maritime trade?
items.answer:  Satavahana coins found across wide regions suggest extensive trade. Many coins specifically depict seafaring ships with masts and sails, indicating that maritime trade was a significant part of their economy.

items.stem: Explain the Satavahana tradition of naming rulers like Gautamiputra Satakarni.
items.answer:  Some Satavahana kings followed a matronymic system, taking their mother’s name first (e.g., ‘Gautamiputra’ means ‘son of Gautami’). This possibly signifies the high status or influence of queens or mothers in their society.

items.stem: What does the Hathigumpha inscription tell us about King Kharavela’s rule?
items.answer:  It records his accomplishments year-by-year, including military victories and public welfare works. It also highlights his devotion to Jainism while claiming tolerance and respect for all sects and sages.

items.stem: What is Sangam literature, and why is it important for historians?
items.answer:  Sangam literature is a collection of ancient Tamil poems from assemblies (Sangams) of poets. It’s the oldest South Indian literature, providing valuable insights into the society, culture, values (love, heroism), and kingdoms (Chola, Chera, Pandya) of that era.

items.stem: Briefly narrate the story of Kannagi from the epic Silappadikaram.
items.answer:  Kannagi’s husband Kovalan wrongly executed in Madurai. She proved his innocence with her matching anklet, causing the shocked Pandya king to die. Kannagi’s curse destroyed Madurai by fire before she was deified.

items.stem: What was the significance of the Kallanai (Grand Anicut) built by Karikala Chola?
items.answer:  The Kallanai was an ancient, complex water diversion structure on the Kaveri river. It irrigated large parts of the delta, enabling extensive rice cultivation and making the region highly productive agriculturally.

items.stem: What goods did the Chera kingdom primarily export, and with whom did they trade?
items.answer:  The Cheras exported valuable goods like spices (pepper), timber, ivory, and pearls. They had extensive trade connections, particularly with the distant Roman Empire and West Asia.

items.stem: How did the Indo-Greek kingdoms emerge in Northwest India?
items.answer:  After Alexander the Great retreated, the Greek governors (satraps) he left behind gradually established their own independent kingdoms in the northwestern regions of the subcontinent, becoming known as the Indo-Greeks.

items.stem: Give an example of cultural blending during the Indo-Greek period.
items.answer:  The Heliodorus pillar near Vidisha, erected by an Indo-Greek ambassador, praises the Indian deity Vasudeva. Indo-Greek coins sometimes depicted Indian deities alongside Greek ones, showing cultural interaction and adoption of local beliefs.

items.stem: What is the Shaka Samvat, and how does it relate to the Gregorian calendar?
items.answer:  The Shaka Samvat is a calendar era developed during the rule of the Shakas (Indo-Scythians). It is India’s National Calendar and runs 78 years behind the internationally used Gregorian calendar (mostly).

items.stem: Describe the extent of the Kushana empire at its peak.
items.answer:  The Kushana empire was vast, stretching from parts of Central Asia through present-day Afghanistan and Pakistan into large parts of northern India, controlling important trade routes like the Silk Route. Downloaded from www.pdf.tube CH 06: The Age of Reorganisation

items.stem: What titles did Kushana king Kanishka use, as seen on his statue’s inscription?
items.answer:  The inscription reads ‘maharaja rajadhiraja devaputra kanishka’, meaning ‘The great king, king of kings, son of God, Kanishka’, indicating lofty claims to power and divine connection.

items.stem: How do Kanishka’s coins reflect religious tolerance or patronage?
items.answer:  His coins depicted not only the emperor but also deities from different traditions, notably Buddha (with Greek script label) and the Hindu god Shiva with Nandi, suggesting patronage or acknowledgement of multiple faiths.

items.stem: What was the Silk Route, and why was controlling parts of it important for the Kushanas?
items.answer:  The Silk Route was a network of ancient trade routes connecting China with the West (Mediterranean) via Central Asia. Controlling sections allowed the Kushanas to tax lucrative trade, boosting their economy and influence.

items.stem: Briefly describe the key difference between the Gandhara and Mathura schools of art.
items.answer:  The Gandhara school (NW India), using grey schist, showed strong Greco-Roman influence (realistic anatomy, flowing robes). The Mathura school (Uttar Pradesh), using red sandstone, reflected a more distinct Indian style (fuller figures, Indian deities).

items.stem: What types of deities were commonly depicted by the Mathura school of art?
items.answer:  The Mathura school depicted a wide range of Indian deities, including figures like Kubera (wealth god), Lakshmi, Shiva, Buddha, as well as yakshas and yakshinis (nature spirits).

items.stem: How did art during the Kushana period lay groundwork for later temple architecture?
items.answer:  This era saw increased development of religious art, including representations of deities that looked more human. This focus on depicting gods and creating dedicated religious imagery paved the way for later, more elaborate temple structures.

items.stem: What major Sanskrit epics were likely composed during this ‘Age of Reorganisation’?
items.answer:  This period saw the flourishing of Sanskrit literature, notably including the composition (or compilation into near-final form) of the great epics, the Mahabharata and the Ramayana.

items.stem: What does the inscription made by the goldsmith Kanhadasa on the Pitalkhora yaksha sculpture suggest?
items.answer:  It suggests that artisans during the Satavahana period might have been skilled in multiple crafts, as a goldsmith also crafted a stone sculpture, indicating versatility in professions.

items.stem: What evidence suggests the Satavahana queen who performed Vedic rituals held significant power?
items.answer:  The Naneghat inscriptions detail her performance of major Vedic rituals (like ashvamedha, usually done by kings) and extensive donations, indicating she wielded considerable religious and political authority as a widow queen.

items.stem: Why was maintaining control over border areas important for kingdoms during this period?
items.answer:  Border areas were constantly contested. Controlling them was crucial for defending the kingdom from attacks by neighbouring rivals or foreign invaders, ensuring the core territory remained secure. NODIA CASE BASED QUESTIO 

items.stem: Archaeologists excavate a site identified as a Satavahana trading post on the west coast. They find Roman pottery shards, Satavahana coins depicting ships, local pottery, and remnants of warehouses. Nearby, inscriptions mention donations made by a local traders’ guild (shreni) to a Buddhist monastery. (i) What does the discovery of Roman pottery indicate about this site? (ii) How do the ship coins and warehouse remnants support the idea of a trading post? (iii) Evaluate the role of the traders’ guild and their relationship with Buddhism, based on the inscription.
items.answer:  (i) It indicates direct or indirect trade connections with the Roman Empire, confirming the Satavahanas’ participation in long-distance maritime trade, likely importing Roman goods. (ii) Ship coins signify the importance of sea trade to the Satavahanas. Warehouses suggest the storage of goods received via ships or awaiting export, characteristic of a trading centre. (iii) The guild’s donation suggests economic prosperity and organized activity among traders. Their support for a Buddhist monastery indicates patronage of religion, possibly for social merit or because Buddhism was popular among mercantile communities, highlighting links between trade, wealth, and religious patronage.

items.stem: A Kushana governor in Mathura needs to commission sculptures for a new temple complex intended to appeal to both local Indian worshippers and officials familiar with Greco- Roman aesthetics from the western parts of the empire. (i) Which local school of art, known for using red sandstone, would be primarily involved? (ii) To incorporate Greco-Roman aesthetics, elements from which other art school might be subtly blended in? (iii) Evaluate the governor’s likely aim in commissioning art that blends styles.
items.answer:  (i) The Mathura school of art, known for using local red sandstone and depicting Indian deities, would be primarily involved. (ii) Elements might be borrowed or adapted from the Gandhara school of art, which was known for its fusion of Indian themes with Greco- Roman stylistic features. (iii) The aim is likely political and cultural integration. By blending styles, the governor acknowledges both local traditions and the broader cultural influences within the diverse Kushana empire, fostering goodwill and reflecting the era’s syncretism.

items.stem: A ruler in the post-Maurya period wants to declare his supremacy over neighbouring territories without engaging in costly wars immediately. He decides to perform a significant Vedic ritual. (i) Which Vedic ritual would be suitable for this purpose? (ii) Explain how performing this ritual asserts the ruler’s power symbolically. (iii) What risk did the ruler take by performing this ritual?
items.answer:  (i) The ashvamedha yajna (horse sacrifice) would be suitable for declaring supremacy over neighbours. (ii) The unchallenged journey of the sacrificial horse through neighbouring territories symbolically represents those rulers’ acceptance of the sponsoring king’s overlordship. Successfully completing the ritual proclaims his paramount status. (iii) The main risk was that a neighbouring ruler might challenge the horse’s passage, forcing the sponsoring king into a battle to prove his claimed supremacy, potentially leading to the war he initially sought to avoid.

items.stem: A historian studying the Sangam Age finds poems describing the bustling port city of Puhar (Kaveripattinam), mentioning Roman ships docking, warehouses full of pepper and pearls awaiting export, and local Chola officials collecting taxes from merchants. (i) What specific economic activities are highlighted in these poems? (ii) What does this description suggest about the Chola kingdom’s economy during this period? (iii) Evaluate the reliability of using poetry like Sangam literature as a source for economic history.
items.answer:  (i) The poems highlight international maritime trade (Roman ships), export of local Click Here to Buy book on Flipkart CH 06: The Age of Reorganisation

items.stem: Analyse the importance of inscriptions (like Hathigumpha, Naneghat, Ashokan edicts revisited) and coins as historical sources for this period.
items.answer:  Inscriptions provide direct accounts of rulers’ achievements, policies, religious beliefs, and administrative actions (Kharavela, Satavahana queen, Ashoka). Coins reveal rulers’ names, titles, timelines, economic conditions (metal used), trade links (find spots), religious affiliations (deities depicted), and artistic styles, offering crucial data where literary sources are scarce.

items.stem: Based on the examples of Satavahana queens and the mention of women fighters against Alexander, evaluate the possible role and status of women during this period.
items.answer:  Evidence suggests varied roles. Satavahana queens (Gautami Balashri, Naneghat queen) wielded considerable influence, performing rituals and issuing inscriptions. The mention of women fighting implies participation beyond domestic spheres in some contexts. However, this limited evidence doesn’t allow generalizations but hints at potentially significant, though diverse, roles for women.

items.stem: Compare the factors contributing to the decline of the Maurya Empire and the Satavahana Empire. Are there common themes?
items.answer:  Both empires faced issues inherent in managing large territories. Weak central control after powerful rulers (Ashoka’s successors, later Satavahanas) allowed regional powers to assert independence. Economic factors (strain of administration/campaigns, potentially economic decline for Satavahanas) also played a role. Thus, weakened central authority and economic pressures seem common themes.

items.stem: How does the story of Kannagi in Silappadikaram reflect societal values concerning justice and a ruler’s dharma?
items.answer:  The story emphasizes the ideal of swift, accurate justice as a ruler’s primary duty (dharma). The Pandya king’s death from shock upon realizing his unjust execution of Kovalan underscores the immense moral weight of a king’s judgement. Kannagi’s transformation and destructive power symbolize the severe consequences when justice fails.

items.stem: Analyse the title ‘Devaputra’ (Son of God) used by Kushana king Kanishka. What might be the purpose of such a title?
items.answer:  This title, likely borrowed from Chinese or other imperial traditions, aimed to elevate the king’s status above ordinary mortals. It suggests a claim to divine mandate or connection, legitimizing his rule, enhancing his authority over diverse subjects, and placing him on par with great emperors of other cultures.

items.stem: Discuss the interplay between warfare and diplomacy (like matrimonial alliances) as methods used by kingdoms to gain power during this period.
items.answer:  Kingdoms used both. Warfare (Pushyamitra vs neighbours, Karikala vs Cheras/Pandyas) aimed at direct conquest and asserting supremacy. Diplomacy, especially matrimonial alliances, was used to build peaceful relationships, secure borders, gain allies against common enemies, and consolidate power without the cost and risk of war. Both were tools in the constant competition.

items.stem: “The ‘Age of Reorganisation’ set the stage for future empires by fostering regional powers and cultural identities.” Evaluate this statement.
items.answer:  This period saw the rise of strong regional kingdoms (Satavahanas, Kushanas, Southern kingdoms) with distinct cultural identities (art, literature, trade specializations). While politically fragmented compared to the Mauryas, these developments created powerful regional bases and rich cultural traditions that would influence and be incorporated into subsequent larger empires like the Guptas. items.stem: Analyse the reasons why the period after the Mauryan decline (c. 185 BCE - 300 CE) is termed the ‘Age of Reorganisation’.
items.answer:  The term reflects profound changes. The unified Maurya empire fragmented, leading to political reorganisation with new regional kingdoms (Shungas, Satavahanas, Chedis, Southern kingdoms) emerging and competing. Simultaneously, foreign invasions (Indo-Greeks, Shakas, Kushanas) led to further political shifts and significant cultural reorganisation through assimilation and interaction.

items.stem: Compare the political strategies used by rulers like Pushyamitra Shunga and Kharavela to assert their authority.
items.answer:  Pushyamitra Shunga used the traditional Vedic ritual, the ashvamedha yajna, signifying military dominance and royal power legitimised through ancient rites. Kharavela, while also highlighting military victories in his inscription, emphasized his adherence to Jain principles and his role as a benevolent ruler respecting all sects, asserting authority through both might and righteousness/ tolerance.

items.stem: “The Satavahana period demonstrates a balance between indigenous traditions and external connections.” Analyse this statement using evidence related to trade and culture.
items.answer:  Satavahanas promoted indigenous culture (Vedic rituals, Prakrit language, local art styles) and unique social customs (matronymics). Simultaneously, they engaged extensively in external trade, reaching the Roman Empire, indicated by coins depicting ships and Roman goods found in their territory. This shows a blend of internal development and outward-looking engagement.

items.stem: Evaluate the significance of the Sangam Age for the history and culture of South India.
items.answer:  The Sangam Age was foundational for South Indian culture. Its literature (oldest Tamil works) provides invaluable insights into the society, values, and politics of the Chola, Chera, and Pandya kingdoms. It established Tamil as a major literary language and documented a distinct cultural identity, influencing regional heritage profoundly.

items.stem: Analyse the process of cultural assimilation as seen during the periods of Indo-Greek and Kushana rule in Northwest India.
items.answer:  Invading groups (Indo-Greeks, Kushanas) brought their own traditions but were significantly influenced by local Indian culture. This resulted in syncretism : rulers adopted Indian religions (Vaishnavism, Buddhism, Shaivism) depicted on coins; art styles fused Greco-Roman and Indian elements (Gandhara); even foreign ambassadors adopted local faiths (Heliodorus). Invaders gradually integrated into the Indian cultural fabric.

items.stem: Explain the development and characteristics of the Gandhara and Mathura schools of art. What do they reveal about the cultural dynamics of the time?
items.answer:  Gandhara art (NW) blended Indian themes with Greco-Roman styles (realism, drapery), using grey schist. Mathura art (North India) used red sandstone, developing a more indigenous Indian aesthetic (fuller figures, local deities). Their coexistence and distinct styles reveal intense cultural interaction alongside strong local artistic traditions during the Kushana period.

items.stem: How did control over sections of the Silk Route benefit the Kushana Empire economically and culturally?
items.answer:  Economically, controlling Silk Route segments allowed Kushanas to tax the lucrative trade between East (China) and West (Rome), generating significant revenue. Culturally, it placed them at a crossroads, facilitating the exchange of goods, ideas, religions (like Buddhism spreading to Central Asia/China), and artistic styles, enriching their diverse empire.

items.stem: King Kanishka issues a gold coin. One side shows the king in ceremonial attire holding a spear. The other side depicts the Buddha standing, with the word ‘BODDO’ inscribed in Greek letters. (i) What does the depiction of the king holding a spear signify? (ii) What does the depiction of Buddha indicate about Kanishka or his empire? (iii) Evaluate the significance of using Greek script for the word ‘Buddha’ on this coin found in India/Central Asia.
items.answer:  (i) It signifies the king’s royal authority and military power, presenting him as a ruler and warrior. (ii) It indicates Kanishka’s patronage, respect, or personal adherence to Buddhism, and reflects the religion’s significant presence and importance within the Kushana empire. (iii) Using Greek script highlights the strong Hellenistic cultural influence still present in the regions ruled by the Kushanas (inherited from Indo-Greeks) and suggests the coin was intended for circulation in areas where Greek script was understood, reflecting the empire’s cultural mix. wwww.nodia.i  Click Here to Buy book on Amazon

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Imagine you receive a letter from someone living in the Gupta Empire. The letter starts like this : “Greetings from Pataliputra! Life here is vibrant and full of excitement. Just yesterday, I witnessed...” Complete the letter with a short paragraph (250-300 words) describing life in the Gupta Empire.
items.answer:  Greetings from Pataliputra! Life here is vibrant and full of excitement. Just yesterday, I witnessed a grand performance at the local theatre, where musicians, dancers, and poets came together to celebrate the spring festival. The streets were filled with colors, laughter, and the smell of incense and sweet dishes. It is truly a wonderful time to live in the Gupta Empire. Our empire is flourishing under the wise and just rule of our emperor, who supports learning, art, and science. The city of Pataliputra is bustling with scholars and traders from distant lands. In the great universities like Nalanda, students study astronomy, mathematics, medicine, and even logic. My cousin is learning Sanskrit literature and often recites verses from Kalidasa, our greatest poet and playwright. Trade is thriving too! Merchants bring silk from China, spices from the south, and even gold and horses from Central Asia. Artisans in the city craft beautiful sculptures and intricate jewelry, while temples and monasteries are being built with fine architecture and carvings. Religion is respected and diverse—though many follow Hinduism and Buddhism, we live peacefully with varied beliefs. Medicine is also advancing—doctors perform Downloaded from www.pdf.tube surgeries and use herbal remedies for treatment. Our calendar is accurate, and scholars have even explained the concept of zero in mathematics! Life is not without its challenges, but there is a sense of pride and stability across the empire. Culture, knowledge, and prosperity surround us, and I feel lucky to be part of this golden age. With warm regards, Vishnugupta Pataliputra, Gupta Empire

items.answer:  Chandragupta II was also known as ‘Vikramaditya’.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: “Periods of peace support the development of various aspects of sociocultural life, literature, and the development of science and technology.’ Examine this statement in the light of the Gupta empire.
items.answer:  The Gupta Empire largely experienced prolonged peace and stability, which allowed for exceptional advancements. Sanskrit literature flourished with writers like Kalidasa. Science and mathematics saw significant contributions from Aryabhata and Varahamihira. Art, architecture (Ajanta, Sarnath), and metallurgy (Iron Pillar) also thrived, supporting the statement.

items.answer:  This is a role-play script activity. Scene : Court of Chandragupta II. Characters : King Vikramaditya, Minister, Scholar Aryabhata, Poet Kalidasa. Vikramaditya : “Esteemed members, report on the empire’s progress.” Minister : “My King, trade prospers, and the new roads ease commerce. The treasury is robust.” Aryabhata : “Maharajadhiraja, my calculations confirm the Earth rotates, explaining day and night.” Kalidasa : “Your Majesty, my new work, Meghadutam, describing the land’s beauty, is complete.” Vikramaditya : “Excellent! Such knowledge and artistry bring glory to our empire.”

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Who were the Pallavas and where did they rule?
items.answer:  The Pallavas were a powerful dynasty that emerged in the south, possibly after the Satavahanas declined. They ruled parts of present-day Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Telangana, and Andhra Pradesh, with their capital at Kanchipuram.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Organise an exploration trip with your teachers to a nearby historical site, museum, or heritage building. After the trip, write a detailed report describing your experience. Include key observations about the site’s historical significance, the architecture, artefacts, and any interesting facts you learned during the visit. Reflect on how the trip enhanced your understanding of history

We saw many old things like statues, coins, tools, and paintings from that time. There were statues of gods and kings made during the Gupta period. The guide told us that the Guptas were great lovers of art, science, and learning. We also saw coins with pictures and writings that showed how rich and advanced the empire was. The museum helped us understand what we read in our book — that the Gupta period was a golden age. People like Kalidasa and Aryabhata lived during this time. I really enjoyed the trip. items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: The period of the Gupta Empire, known for significant developments in art, literature, and science, is often referred to by what term by some historians?
items.answer:  (B) The Classical Age of India The Gupta period is frequently called the ‘classical age’ of India by some historians due to remarkable achievements in fields like art, architecture, literature, science, and mathematics, setting high standards and leaving a lasting legacy.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: What does the remarkable rust resistance of the Iron Pillar of Delhi, after over 1,600 years, primarily indicate about ancient Indian technology? processing

options.label: A
options.text: The use of imported rust-proof metals only

options.label: C
options.text: A climate that naturally prevents rusting

items.answer:  (B) Advanced knowledge of metallurgy and processing The Iron Pillar’s minimal corrosion over centuries showcases ancient India’s sophisticated understanding of metallurgy, including the creation of iron alloys with unique properties that form a protective passive layer against rust.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: What does the title ‘maharajadhiraja’, adopted by Gupta rulers, literally mean?

options.label: A
options.text: Lord of the entire known universe

options.label: B
options.text: Great king of all other kings

options.label: C
options.text: The chosen one of the gods

items.answer:  (B) Great king of all other kings The title ‘maharajadhiraja’ translates to “great king of kings.” Gupta emperors adopted such grand titles to signify their supreme authority and imperial status over other subordinate rulers and territories within their domain.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Chandragupta I, an early Gupta ruler, is remembered for his strategic alliances. He married Kumaradevi, a princess from which influential clan?
items.answer:  (B) The Lichchhavi clan Chandragupta I strengthened his political position through a matrimonial alliance with the powerful Lichchhavi clan by marrying Princess Kumaradevi. This alliance was crucial for the early expansion and consolidation of Gupta power.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: How did the Gupta ruler Samudragupta’s approach to defeated kings in the south differ from his approach to rulers in Aryavarta (northern India)? northern ones northern ones Click Here to Buy book on Flipkart

options.label: C
options.text: He exiled all defeated kings from south

options.label: D
options.text: He formed equal alliances with all regions

items.answer:  (B) He reinstated southern kings; annexed northern ones Samudragupta’s Prayaga Prashasti indicates that he uprooted rulers in Aryavarta (northern India), incorporating their territories directly. However, he often reinstated defeated southern kings, allowing them to rule as tributaries.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: The Prayaga Prashasti, an inscription praising Samudragupta’s achievements, was authored by whom?

options.label: A
options.text: Kalidasa, the great poet and dramatist

options.label: C
options.text: Harisena, his court poet and minister

items.answer:  (C) Harisena, his court poet and minister The Prayaga Prashasti (Allahabad Pillar Inscription) is a eulogy detailing the conquests and qualities of Samudragupta. It was composed by Harisena, who was a prominent poet and a high-ranking minister in Samudragupta’s court.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Samudragupta’s ambition, according to the Prayaga Prashasti, was to achieve ‘dharani- bandha’, which means to _____ the Earth.
items.answer:  (C) unify The term ‘dharani-bandha’ mentioned in the Prayaga Prashasti describes Samudragupta’s ambition to unify the Earth, signifying his imperial aspiration to bring vast territories under his single, overarching rule and control.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Faxian’s travelogue mentions that heads of Vaishya families established houses for charity and medicines where the poor and sick were cared for. This observation highlights what aspect of Gupta society? neglect

options.label: A
options.text: The government’s complete control over welfare

options.label: B
options.text: The prevalence of widespread poverty and

options.label: C
options.text: The role of community philanthropy, charity

options.label: D
options.text: The absence of any medical facilities

items.answer:  (C) The role of community philanthropy, charity Faxian’s account of Vaishya families providing charitable services, including medical care for the needy, points to a societal value of philanthropy and community responsibility for welfare, alongside any state provisions during that time.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: What was a ‘prashasti’ in ancient India, like the one for Samudragupta at Prayaga?

options.label: A
options.text: A type of tax collected from farmers

options.label: B
options.text: A royal decree establishing new city

options.label: C
options.text: A eulogy or inscription praising a ruler

options.label: D
options.text: A manual for military strategy or war

items.answer:  (C) A eulogy or inscription praising a ruler A ‘prashasti’ is a type of inscription, often found on pillars or temple walls, composed in praise of a king or ruler. These texts typically eulogize the ruler’s achievements, virtues, and conquests.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: The Gupta rulers’ use of grand titles like ‘chakravartin’ primarily aimed to achieve what?

options.label: B
options.text: To emphasize their supreme authority, power

options.label: C
options.text: To indicate their foreign origins to people

options.label: D
options.text: To reduce the amount of tax collected

items.answer:  (B) To emphasize their supreme authority, power Titles such as ‘maharajadhiraja’ (great king of kings) and ‘chakravartin’ (universal emperor) were adopted by Gupta rulers to project an image of supreme power, vast dominion, and superiority over other contemporary rulers. NODIA CH 07: The Gupta Era : An Age of Tireless Creativity

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Prabhavati Gupta, daughter of Chandragupta II, was married into which neighboring royal family, strengthening Gupta alliances?

options.label: A
options.text: The Pallava kingdom to their south

options.label: B
options.text: The Vakataka kingdom to their south

options.label: C
options.text: The Shaka kingdom to their west

options.label: D
options.text: The Kamarupa kingdom to their east

items.answer:  (B) The Vakataka kingdom to their south Prabhavati Gupta, an influential Gupta princess, was married to a prince of the Vakataka kingdom, which was located to the south of the Gupta empire. This matrimonial alliance was strategically important for both dynasties.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Which of the following correctly pairs a Gupta era personality with their primary field of contribution?
items.answer:  (D) Varahamihira - Astronomy, astrology, science Varahamihira was a distinguished polymath of the Gupta period, known for his encyclopedic work ‘Brihat Samhita,’ which covered diverse subjects including astronomy, astrology, meteorology, and other scientific topics.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Assertion (A) : The Gupta period is often called a ‘classical age’ due to significant achievements in art, science, and literature. Reason (R) : This cultural efflorescence was primarily due to continuous external invasions stimulating creativity. explanation of A. correct explanation of A.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer:  (C) A is true, but R is false The Gupta period is indeed considered a classical age because of its remarkable cultural and intellectual achievements. However, this flourishing was largely facilitated by a long period of relative peace and internal stability, not continuous external invasions.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Which of the following Gupta era contributions is INCORRECTLY matched with its description? ancient metallurgy dramatic theory only achievements Buddhist learning
items.answer:  (B) Aryabhatiya (by Aryabhata) - Treatise on dramatic theory only Aryabhata’s ‘Aryabhatiya’ is a seminal work on mathematics and astronomy, proposing concepts like Earth’s rotation and providing calculations for eclipses. It is not primarily a treatise on dramatic theory.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: The rulers exclusively patronized Vaishnavism, suppressing other faiths. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.answer:  (A) 2 only The Gupta capital was at Pataliputra. They did have extensive trade with Southeast Asia and beyond. While many Gupta rulers were Vaishnavas, they generally practiced religious tolerance and patronized other faiths like Buddhism.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Aryabhata, a prominent mathematician and astronomer of the Gupta period, proposed that the Earth _____ on its axis, explaining day and night.
items.answer:  (B) spins Aryabhata made significant contributions, including the revolutionary idea for his time that NODIA (A) 1 only (B) 1 and 2 (C) 2 and 3 (D) 1, 2, 3

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: The Kamarupa kingdom, ruled by the Varman dynasty during the Gupta period, was located in the valley of the _____ River.
items.answer:  (C) Brahmaputra The Kamarupa kingdom, an important power in northeastern India contemporary with the Guptas, was situated in the fertile valley of the Brahmaputra River, corresponding broadly to modern-day Assam and surrounding regions.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: What is a “regent ruler” in the context of a kingdom?

options.label: A
options.text: A king who has conquered many new lands

options.label: B
options.text: A ruler who governs temporarily for monarch

options.label: C
options.text: A religious leader who advises the true king

options.label: D
options.text: A foreign ambassador residing in the capital

items.answer:  (B) A ruler who governs temporarily for monarch A regent is a person appointed to administer a state because the monarch is a minor, is absent, or is incapacitated. Prabhavati Gupta, for instance, acted as regent ruler of the Vakataka kingdom.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Varahamihira’s encyclopedic work, the Brihat Samhita, covered a wide range of subjects including astronomy, astrology, and what other practical field?
items.answer:  (C) Weather forecasting Varahamihira’s Brihat Samhita was a comprehensive work that touched upon diverse topics. Besides astronomy and astrology, it included sections on meteorology and weather forecasting, architecture, and even agriculture, reflecting his wide knowledge.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: The fact that Gupta land grants were often inscribed on copper plates suggests an emphasis on what administrative practice? keeping

options.label: A
options.text: Keeping transactions secret from the public

options.label: B
options.text: Using the most inexpensive recording means

options.label: D
options.text: Making documents easily alterable if needed

items.answer:  (C) Ensuring accurate and permanent record- keeping Inscribing land grants on durable materials like copper plates was a method to create accurate, official, and lasting records of these important administrative and economic transactions, ensuring their legitimacy and preventing disputes over them.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: What were ‘ghatikas’ in the context of ancient South Indian kingdoms like the Pallavas?

options.label: A
options.text: Fortified military garrisons on the borders

options.label: B
options.text: Royal treasuries for storing valuable jewels

options.label: C
options.text: Centers of learning and higher education

options.label: D
options.text: Special courts for resolving trade disputes

items.answer:  (C) Centers of learning and higher education ‘Ghatikas’ were prominent centers of advanced learning and education, particularly flourishing under dynasties like the Pallavas in South India. These institutions played a crucial role in fostering intellectual and scholarly pursuits in various subjects.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: How did the Gupta empire’s system of administration often manage provincial areas regarding local rulers?

options.label: A
options.text: By replacing all local rulers with officials

options.label: B
options.text: By granting land to local rulers, chiefs

items.answer:  (B) By granting land to local rulers, chiefs The Gupta administration often divided the empire into provinces and granted land (and authority) to local rulers, priests, or chieftains. These grants, recorded on copper plates, allowed for decentralized governance while ensuring loyalty and revenue.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Which ancient Indian scholar is correctly paired with their significant literary or scientific work? text text

options.label: C
options.text: Aryabhata - Wrote the epic Meghadutam tale

items.answer:  (D) Charaka - Associated with Charaka Samhita text The Charaka Samhita is a foundational text of Ayurveda, and Charaka is traditionally credited as one of its principal compilers/authors. Faxian wrote a travelogue, Kalidasa wrote Meghadutam, and Aryabhata authored Aryabhatiya.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Assertion (A) : The Gupta rulers, while often Vaishnavas, generally patronized other religious traditions like Buddhism and Jainism. Reason (R) : This policy of religious tolerance contributed to the cultural and intellectual vibrancy of the Gupta period. explanation of A. correct explanation of A.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer:  (A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Gupta emperors, despite personal Vaishnava faith, largely adopted a policy of religious tolerance, supporting Buddhist institutions like Nalanda and allowing various faiths to flourish. This inclusivity fostered a rich cultural and intellectual environment.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Which Gupta era achievement is INCORRECTLY linked to its field? Astronomy poetry design medicine

options.label: C
options.text: Iron Pillar of Delhi - Advanced architectural

items.answer:  (C) Iron Pillar of Delhi - Advanced architectural design While the Iron Pillar is an architectural marvel in terms of its construction and placement, its most celebrated achievement lies in the field of metallurgy, specifically its rust-resistant properties, rather than primarily its architectural design.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: What does ‘Ayurveda’, which was codified during the Gupta period, refer to? mainly

options.label: A
options.text: A system of ancient Indian temple architecture

options.label: B
options.text: A traditional Indian system of medicine

options.label: C
options.text: A school of classical Indian dance forms

options.label: D
options.text: A collection of ancient Indian epic poems

items.answer:  (B) A traditional Indian system of medicine mainly Ayurveda is a comprehensive traditional system of medicine with historical roots in the Indian subcontinent. Key Ayurvedic texts like the Charaka Samhita and Sushruta Samhita were compiled and given final shape during the Gupta era.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: The famous Ajanta Caves, known for their exquisite murals and rock-cut architecture, received patronage from the Guptas and which other contemporary dynasty?
items.answer:  (C) The Vakatakas of Deccan The magnificent Ajanta Caves, a UNESCO World Heritage site, were developed over centuries. Significant phases of their creation, including many murals and sculptures, occurred with the patronage of the Gupta emperors and the contemporary Vakataka dynasty.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: The depiction of Samudragupta as a veena player on his coins primarily suggests what about his personality or reign?

options.label: A
options.text: His sole interest was in musical performance

options.label: B
options.text: His kingdom’s economy was based on music

options.label: C
options.text: His appreciation and patronage of the arts

options.label: D
options.text: His military weakness and focus on leisure

items.answer:  (C) His appreciation and patronage of the arts Portraying a powerful emperor like Samudragupta playing the veena (a musical instrument) on coins was a way to showcase his cultured nature and his support for the arts, beyond just his military conquests and administrative capabilities.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: A historian is studying an ancient Indian text that discusses formulas for planetary motions, a near-accurate length of the year, and a correct explanation for eclipses. This text is most likely the work of which Gupta era scholar known to us? the great mathematician- astronomer

options.label: A
options.text: Kalidasa, the poet and the great dramatist

options.label: C
options.text: Harisena, the court poet of Samudragupta

items.answer:  (D) Aryabhata, the great mathematician- astronomer These scientific contributions – formulas for planetary motion, accurate calculation of the year’s length, and the correct explanation of solar and lunar eclipses – are hallmark achievements of Aryabhata, as detailed in his work, the Aryabhatiya.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Which of the following was NOT a significant factor contributing to the decline of the Gupta Empire? rulers

options.label: A
options.text: External invasions by groups like the Hunas

options.label: B
options.text: The rise of powerful regional independent

options.label: C
options.text: A complete lack of trade with any region

items.answer:  (C) A complete lack of trade with any region The decline of the Gupta Empire was due to factors like Huna invasions, the assertion of independence by regional rulers, and possibly internal succession struggles. While trade might have been affected, a complete cessation was not the primary cause.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Kanchipuram, known as the ‘city of a thousand temples’ and a major center of learning, was the capital of which South Indian dynasty contemporary to the later Guptas?
items.answer:  (D) The Pallava dynasty Kanchipuram served as the illustrious capital of the Pallava dynasty. It became a significant political, religious (especially Shaivite and Vaishnavite), and educational center in South Click Here to Buy book on Amazon CH 07: The Gupta Era : An Age of Tireless Creativity (D) Pataliputra - Known for its shipbuilding industry

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: A visitor to ancient India observes magnificent temples with intricate carvings of Hindu deities, advanced astronomical observatories, and scholars actively engaged in mathematical research and composing Sanskrit poetry. These observations are most characteristic of which flourishing historical period in India?

options.label: A
options.text: The early Vedic period of sacrifices

items.answer:  (C) The Gupta (“Classical”) period These features – flourishing temple architecture, advancements in astronomy and mathematics, and a vibrant Sanskrit literary tradition – are all hallmarks of the Gupta period, often referred to as India’s “classical age” or “golden age”.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Which of these was NOT a major center for artistic production or learning specifically highlighted during the Gupta and contemporary periods?
items.answer:  (C) Mohenjo-daro (Harappan seals, pottery) Mohenjo-daro was a major city of the much earlier Indus Valley (Harappan) Civilization (c. 2500- 1900 BCE). Sarnath, Ajanta, and Kanchipuram were significant centers during the Gupta era and contemporary periods for art and learning.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: The Gupta Empire flourished primarily between which centuries?
items.answer:  (B) 3rd to 6th century CE The Gupta Empire rose to prominence around the early 4th century CE (with early rulers in the 3rd century CE) and flourished as a major power in India until its decline in the mid-6th century CE.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: What does the term ‘codified’ mean, as in ‘Ayurveda got codified during the Gupta period’? languages

options.label: B
options.text: Kept secret and known only to few

options.label: C
options.text: Arranged or written in an organized way

options.label: D
options.text: Discovered for the very first time

items.answer:  (C) Arranged or written in an organized way To ‘codify’ something, like a system of knowledge or laws, means to arrange it systematically, often by writing it down in an organized and comprehensive manner. Foundational Ayurvedic texts were given their final, organized form during this time.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: How did the political situation in India generally change after the decline of the Kushana Empire leading to the rise of the Guptas? war

options.label: A
options.text: From unified rule to further fragmentation

options.label: B
options.text: From regional powers to a new consolidation

options.label: C
options.text: From foreign domination to complete isolation

options.label: D
options.text: From peaceful states to constant widespread

items.answer:  (B) From regional powers to a new consolidation After the weakening of the Kushana Empire, which controlled northern India, new regional powers emerged. The Guptas rose from among these, initiating a fresh period of political consolidation and empire-building.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: The Gupta ruler Chandragupta II was also famously known by the title _____.
items.answer:  (C) Vikramaditya Chandragupta II, one of the most illustrious Gupta emperors, adopted the prestigious title ‘Vikramaditya,’ meaning “Sun of Prowess.” This title is associated with legendary tales of wisdom, justice, and patronage of arts. NODIA

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: The Prayaga Prashasti describes Samudragupta as a skilled musician, particularly a player of which instrument, as also depicted on some of his coins?
items.answer:  (C) Veena (Lute) Some of Samudragupta’s gold coins depict him playing the veena, a traditional Indian stringed instrument. This, along with descriptions in the Prayaga Prashasti, highlights his accomplishments beyond warfare, including his proficiency in music.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: A scholar in ancient Pataliputra around 500 CE writes a treatise correctly explaining that lunar eclipses occur when the Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon, casting a shadow. This scholar is most likely :
items.answer:  (B) Aryabhata Aryabhata, in his work Aryabhatiya, provided scientifically accurate explanations for both solar and lunar eclipses, correctly identifying that a lunar eclipse happens when the Earth’s shadow falls on the Moon.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Which Gupta-era figure or text is INCORRECTLY matched with its primary domain? Mechanics
items.answer:  (B) Varahamihira - Poetry and Dramatic Arts Varahamihira was a renowned astronomer, mathematician, and astrologer, known for works like the Brihat Samhita. While learned, his primary domain was not poetry and dramatic arts, which was more Kalidasa’s forte.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Assertion (A) : The Gupta period witnessed significant advancements in Indian mathematics, including the concept of zero and the decimal system. Reason (R) : These mathematical innovations had limited impact and were not transmitted to other parts of the world. explanation of A. correct explanation of A.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer:  (C) A is true, but R is false The Gupta period was indeed a time of major mathematical advancements in India, including the development of the concept of zero and the decimal place value system. These innovations were profoundly impactful and were later transmitted to other cultures.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: The Charaka Samhita primarily dealt with astronomical calculations. Which of the above statements is/are correct for that?
items.answer:  (A) 1 and 2 only Kalidasa is renowned for his Sanskrit literary works. Aryabhata made significant mathematical contributions, including an accurate approximation of pi. The Charaka Samhita is a foundational text of Ayurveda (medicine), not astronomy.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: The Gupta rulers were generally devout followers of the Hindu deity _____, whose mount Garuda often appears in their iconography.
items.answer:  (C) Vishnu Many Gupta emperors were ardent devotees of Vishnu (Vaishnavas). This is reflected in their Downloaded from www.pdf.tube CH 07: The Gupta Era : An Age of Tireless Creativity inscriptions, coinage (e.g., Lakshmi, Vishnu’s consort, appearing), and the frequent depiction of Garuda, Vishnu’s divine eagle mount.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: What does the term ‘outcastes’ (like the chandalas mentioned by Faxian) signify in a social context?

options.label: A
options.text: People who willingly choose to live alone

options.label: B
options.text: Foreign merchants residing outside city walls

options.label: C
options.text: Individuals belonging to the highest royal

options.label: D
options.text: People rejected from a social group

items.answer:  (D) People rejected from a social group ‘Outcastes’ refer to individuals or groups who are rejected, excluded, or considered outside the pale of the established social hierarchy or varna system. Faxian’s account indicates the chandalas faced such exclusion.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: The Pallava dynasty, which rose to prominence in South India, had its capital at which city?
items.answer:  (C) Kanchipuram Kanchipuram was the celebrated capital of the Pallava dynasty. It developed into a major political, cultural, and religious center, renowned for its magnificent temples and as a hub of learning in South India.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: The establishment of ‘ghatikas’ by dynasties like the Pallavas indicates their commitment to what aspect of society?

options.label: A
options.text: Expanding their military strength and power

options.label: D
options.text: Enforcing strict religious uniformity on all

items.answer:  (C) Fostering education and intellectual growth Ghatikas were centers of higher learning and education. The establishment and support of such institutions by rulers like the Pallavas demonstrate their commitment to fostering intellectual pursuits, scholarship, and the advancement of knowledge.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: How did Samudragupta’s policy towards the Kamarupa kingdom generally mirror his policy towards the Pallavas? empire rulers

options.label: A
options.text: He directly annexed both kingdoms into

options.label: B
options.text: He formed matrimonial alliances with both

options.label: C
options.text: He defeated them but allowed them rule

options.label: D
options.text: He ignored both, focusing on western India

items.answer:  (C) He defeated them but allowed them rule According to the Prayaga Prashasti, Samudragupta defeated rulers in both the Pallava kingdom (south) and the Kamarupa kingdom (northeast). However, instead of directly annexing these distant territories, he often allowed their rulers to continue governing as tributaries, acknowledging his overlordship.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Which Gupta period text is correctly matched with its primary subject matter? mathematics stories love techniques

options.label: B
options.text: Brihat Samhita - A collection of epic war

options.label: C
options.text: Aryabhatiya - A Sanskrit play about royal

options.label: D
options.text: Sushruta Samhita - A text on surgical

items.answer:  (D) Sushruta Samhita - A text on surgical techniques The Sushruta Samhita is an ancient Sanskrit text on medicine and surgery, considered one of the foundational works of Ayurveda. It provides detailed descriptions of various surgical procedures, instruments, and medical knowledge.

items.stem: Analyse the significance of the Gupta administrative system involving land grants to local rulers/chieftains.
items.answer:  This decentralized approach allowed efficient governance over a vast empire. It ensured tax collection and local administration without direct central control everywhere, fostering loyalty (or potential future independence) among local elites. Copper plate records provided administrative permanence and legal validity to these grants.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: How did thriving trade networks, both internal and external, contribute to the prosperity and cultural vibrancy of the Gupta ‘classical age’?
items.answer:  Trade generated wealth through taxes and commerce, funding the state, supporting artisans, and enabling patronage of arts and sciences. External trade brought in resources and facilitated cultural exchange (ideas, technologies, artistic influences) with regions like Rome, SE Asia, and China, contributing to the era’s dynamism and cosmopolitanism.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Analyse the relationship between political stability under the Guptas and the flourishing of science, literature, and art.
items.answer:  Relative peace and political stability created a secure environment. Economic prosperity allowed rulers and elites to patronize scholars (Aryabhata, Varahamihira), writers (Kalidasa), and artists (Ajanta, Sarnath). This support, combined with intellectual ferment and consolidation of past knowledge, enabled significant creative and scientific advancements.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Compare the scientific contributions of Aryabhata and Varahamihira. What different approaches or areas did they focus on?
items.answer:  Aryabhata focused on foundational mathematical principles and theoretical astronomy, making precise calculations (year length, eclipses) and proposing revolutionary ideas (Earth’s rotation). Varahamihira had a more encyclopedic approach, compiling knowledge across diverse applied sciences – astronomy, astrology, architecture, weather, agriculture – blending observation with traditional wisdom.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: “Gupta rulers, while patrons of Vaishnavism, practiced religious tolerance.” Evaluate this statement.
items.answer:  Evidence supports this. Gupta rulers were Vaishnavas (Vishnu devotees, seen on coins/ inscriptions). However, they patronized Buddhist institutions like Nalanda University and monks. Figures like Samudragupta were praised for supporting learning generally. This suggests a policy of tolerance and support for various prevailing religious and philosophical traditions.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Analyse the key characteristics of Gupta-era art and architecture, using examples like the Sarnath Buddha or Ajanta caves.
items.answer:  Gupta art emphasized harmony, elegance, and idealized forms, moving towards classical refinement. Sarnath Buddhas show serenity and perfect balance. Ajanta caves showcase mastery in both sculpture and vibrant mural painting (narrative scenes, detailed figures). Early structural temples (like Deogarh) also began appearing, showing architectural innovation.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: How did the political situation in North India (Gupta decline, Huna invasions) differ from that in the South (Pallava rise) around the 6th century CE?
items.answer:  In the North, the large Gupta empire was weakening and fragmenting due to invasions (Hunas) and internal factors. In contrast, the South saw the consolidation and rise of a major regional power, the Pallavas, who were building their own influence, possibly benefiting from the decline of earlier powers like the Satavahanas.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity

items.answer:  Kanchipuram served as the Pallava capital and became a major political, religious, and educational centre. The moniker ‘city of a thousand temples’ reflects the extensive temple-building patronage by Pallava rulers (mostly Shiva devotees), making it a crucial hub for South Indian art, architecture, and learning (housing ghatikas). items.stem: What were the main causes of the Gupta Empire’s decline?
items.answer:  Decline was caused by repeated invasions from external groups like the Hunas weakening the empire, combined with the rise of powerful regional rulers challenging central authority, leading to internal conflicts and fragmentation.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Who were the Pallavas, and where was their capital?
items.answer:  The Pallavas were a powerful dynasty ruling parts of South India after the Satavahanas. Their capital was Kanchipuram in present-day Tamil Nadu, known as a major learning centre.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: What were the Pallavas known for in terms of cultural contributions?
items.answer:  They were great patrons of art and architecture, credited with magnificent Dravidian-style temples and rock-cut caves, particularly dedicated to Shiva. They also fostered learning through centres like ghatikas.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Which dynasty ruled the Kamarupa kingdom in the Northeast during this time?
items.answer:  The Varman dynasty ruled the Kamarupa kingdom, covering areas of modern Assam and neighbouring regions.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: How did Samudragupta deal with defeated rulers in the South (Pallavas) and Northeast (Kamarupa)?
items.answer:  He adopted a policy of reinstating defeated rulers. He let them keep their thrones provided they accepted his overlordship and paid tribute, maintaining relations without direct annexation.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Why is the Gupta legacy considered important for India today?
items.answer:  The Gupta era made foundational contributions in science, math (decimal system implicit in Aryabhata’s work), medicine (Ayurveda), literature (Kalidasa, Puranas), and art/ architecture that deeply influenced subsequent Indian culture and traditions.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: What evidence suggests the presence of Indian traders on Socotra Island?
items.answer:  Archaeological finds on Socotra include Indian pottery, inscriptions in the Brahmi script, and architectural designs like a Buddhist stupa, indicating a sustained presence of Indian traders over centuries. LONG ANSWER QUESTIO 

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Analyse the strategies used by Gupta rulers like Chandragupta I and Samudragupta to build and consolidate their empire.
items.answer:  Chandragupta I used strategic matrimonial alliances (e.g., with Lichchhavis) and possibly initial military gains to establish a base. Samudragupta employed extensive military campaigns (‘dharani- bandha’ ambition), defeating numerous kings but also using diplomacy by reinstating tributary rulers, creating a vast but manageable empire praised in the Prayaga Prashasti.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: “The Prayaga Prashasti is a biased source, yet historically valuable.” Analyse this statement.
items.answer:  It’s biased because it was composed by a court poet (Harisena) specifically to praise Samudragupta, likely exaggerating his virtues and victories. However, it’s valuable as it provides contemporary details on his campaigns, the names of defeated kings/regions, Gupta administration ideals, and the king’s cultural patronage (like music).

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Evaluate Faxian’s account as a source for understanding Gupta society. What are its strengths and limitations?
items.answer:  Strength : Provides a unique contemporary, external perspective on prosperity, administration, charity, and urban life in the Gangetic plains. Limitation : Reflects a visitor’s perspective, possibly focusing on favourable aspects or specific regions/classes, and might miss nuances or negative aspects (like the brief mention of outcastes suggests). It requires corroboration. NODIA

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Explain the significance of titles like ‘maharajadhiraja’ adopted by Gupta rulers.
items.answer:  These grand titles (‘great king of kings’) signified supreme authority and imperial status, claiming superiority over rulers with simpler titles like ‘rajan’, reflecting the Guptas’ vast power and ambition.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: How did the Gupta system of administration balance central control and local autonomy?
items.answer:  The empire was divided into provinces. While the emperor held supreme authority, land grants were given to local rulers/chieftains who managed their regions and collected taxes, recorded on copper plates.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Describe the scope of India’s trade during the Gupta era.
items.answer:  Trade was extensive, both internally and externally. India traded textiles, spices, ivory, and gems with the Mediterranean world (via routes possibly including Socotra), Southeast Asia, and China.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: How did the Gupta rulers demonstrate religious tolerance despite being Vaishnavas?
items.answer:  Although devotees of Vishnu, they patronised other traditions. They supported Buddhist institutions like Nalanda University and various monasteries (viharas), fostering an inclusive religious environment.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Why is the Gupta period often called India’s ‘classical age’?
items.answer:  Due to relative peace and stability, the period saw exceptional flourishing in Sanskrit literature (Kalidasa), science/mathematics (Aryabhata, Varahamihira), art/architecture (Ajanta, Gupta temples), and philosophy, setting high standards and consolidating past knowledge.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Summarize Aryabhata’s key contributions to astronomy.
items.answer:  Aryabhata proposed Earth spins on its axis (explaining day/night), calculated the year’s length accurately, correctly explained solar/lunar eclipses, and provided formulas for planetary motions.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: What range of subjects did Varahamihira cover in his Brihat Samhita?
items.answer:  His encyclopedic work covered diverse subjects including astronomy, astrology, mathematics, geography, weather forecasting, architecture, water divination, agriculture, and gemology, reflecting wide-ranging scholarship.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Briefly explain the story of Kalidasa’s Meghadutam (‘The Cloud Messenger’).
items.answer:  A banished yaksha asks a passing cloud to carry a message of love and longing to his beloved wife far away, allowing Kalidasa to poetically describe landscapes across North India.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: What is the focus of Ayurveda, as codified in texts like Charaka Samhita?
items.answer:  Ayurveda focuses on holistic healing, emphasizing the connection between mind, body, and nature. The texts cover disease diagnosis, treatments, medicines, diet, and even surgical techniques.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Name two important centres known for Gupta- era art.
items.answer:  Sarnath (Uttar Pradesh), known for refined Buddha sculptures, and the Ajanta caves (Maharashtra), famous for their murals and sculptures, are key centres. Udayagiri (MP) is also noted.

items.chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
items.stem: Describe the typical aesthetic qualities of Gupta art.
items.answer:  Gupta art is known for its balance, harmony, refined elegance, idealized human forms (especially Buddha images from Sarnath showing serenity), and detailed craftsmanship, setting high aesthetic standards.
